Transcriptomic Response to Influenza A Infection in Mouse Cerebellum

Princess

date: “2026-07-27” output: html_document: —

Introduction

Influenza A virus (IAV) infection induces extensive molecular and cellular responses within the host. Although IAV primarily targets the respiratory system, infection can also produce systemic inflammation and neurological complications. Nevertheless, the effects of IAV infection on gene expression within the central nervous system remain less well characterized than its effects in respiratory and peripheral immune tissues.

The cerebellum is traditionally associated with motor coordination but also participates in broader neurological and immunological processes. Examining transcriptional changes in cerebellar tissue may therefore provide insight into how respiratory viral infection influences the brain, even in the absence of direct viral replication within neural tissue.

This study analyzed the GSE96870 RNA-sequencing dataset to characterize the cerebellar transcriptomic response to IAV infection. Gene-expression profiles were compared among uninfected mice and mice collected at 4 and 8 days post-infection. The objectives were to evaluate global similarities among samples, identify differentially expressed genes, and determine the biological processes and pathways associated with the observed transcriptional changes.

Methods

Data Acquisition

Raw RNA-seq data was downloaded from NCBI SRA using prefetch and converted to FASTQ format using fastq-dump (SRA Toolkit v3.4.1). The dataset comprises 9 paired-end samples (SRR5364316, SRR5364317, SRR5364322, SRR5364318, SRR5364319, SRR5364323, SRR5364321, SRR5364325, SRR5364330).

Quality Control

Raw reads were assessed using FastQC. All samples showed high quality scores (Phred > 30) across read lengths with minimal adapter contamination, indicating no trimming was necessary.

Alignment

Reads were aligned to the Mus musculus reference genome (GRCm39, Ensembl release 116) using HISAT2. All samples achieved 100% overall alignment rates, confirming high-quality alignments.

Read Counting

Read counts were generated using featureCounts with the GRCm39 GTF annotation file. Count matrices were merged across all 9 samples for downstream analysis.

Differential Expression Analysis

Differential expression analysis was performed using DESeq2 in R. Three comparisons were made: - Flu4 vs Control (Day 4 infected vs non-infected) - Flu8 vs Control (Day 8 infected vs non-infected) - Flu8 vs Flu4 (Day 8 vs Day 4 infected)

Genes with |log2FoldChange| > 1 and adjusted p-value < 0.05 were considered significant. LFC shrinkage was applied using the ashr method.

Pathway Enrichment Analysis

GO Biological Process and KEGG pathway enrichment analyses were performed using clusterProfiler with the org.Mm.eg.db annotation database.

Results

Principal Component Analysis

Principal component analysis was used to examine the major sources of gene-expression variation across the nine samples. Principal component analysis showed that PC1 and PC2 explained 40% and 34% of the variance, respectively. The samples did not cluster completely by condition,two Flu8 samples clustered closely, while the third was separated along PC1. Similarly, one control sample and one Flu4 sample were distinct from their respective group replicates.

PCA of VST-transformed counts

Sample Distance Heatmap

Pairwise sample distances were visualized to further evaluate similarities among the expression profiles. The sample-distance heatmap showed that the three Flu8 samples clustered together, indicating relatively similar expression profiles. Two control samples also clustered closely, whereas the third control sample was more similar to some Flu4 samples. The Flu4 group showed greater variability among replicates.

Sample Distance Heatmap

Differential Expression Results

The differential gene expression varied substantially across the three comparisons relative to control. At day 4 post-infection,14 genes were significantly including 10 upregulated and 4 downregulated genes. By day 8, the number of differentially expressed genes increased to 254 genes, comprising 147 upregulated and 107 downregulated genes.

The direct comparison between day 8 and day 4 identified 80 genes differentially expressed genes, including 53 upregulated and 27 downregulated genes.

Volcano Plots

Volcano plots were used to visualize the relationship between gene-expression effect size and statistical significance for each comparison. The day-4 comparison contained relatively few genes that simultaneously exceeded the fold-change and adjusted p-value thresholds. In contrast, the day-8 comparison showed a substantially larger set of significantly altered genes, with both positive and negative expression changes.The day-8 versus day-4 comparison also identified significant expression differences.

Top DEG Heatmap

The top 50 genes from the Flu4-versus-control comparison showed distinct expression differences between the groups. Control samples clustered together, while Flu4 samples displayed both increased and decreased expression across separate gene clusters. Flu8 samples showed more variable and generally intermediate expression patterns

Gene Ontology Biological Process Enrichment

Gene Ontology Biological Process enrichment analysis identified several interferon-associated processes among the differentially expressed genes.

The most significantly enriched term was response to interferon-beta (GO:0035456; adjusted p = 9.67 × 10-6). Other significantly enriched terms included response to type II interferon (GO:0034341; adjusted p = 6.32 × 10-5), cellular response to interferon-beta (GO:0035458; adjusted p = 1.63 × 10-4), and cellular response to type II interferon (GO:0071346; adjusted p = 1.40 × 10-3). Response to toxic substance was also enriched (GO:0009636; adjusted p = 4.55 × 10-3).

GO Biological Process Enrichment

KEGG Enrichment Pathway

KEGG pathway analysis identified a smaller set of significantly enriched metabolic pathways. Ether lipid metabolism was the most significantly enriched pathway (mmu00565; adjusted p = 2.25 × 10-4). Alpha-linolenic acid metabolism (mmu00592; adjusted p = 1.66 × 10-2) and linoleic acid metabolism (mmu00591; adjusted p = 2.48 × 10-2) were also significantly enriched.

KEGG Pathway Enrichment

Discussion

This analysis showed that the transcriptomic response to influenza A infection in the mouse cerebellum became more pronounced over time. Differential expression was limited at Day 4 but increased substantially by Day 8, indicating that the effect of infection intensified as it progressed. The Flu8-versus-Flu4 comparison supported this pattern by showing that gene expression continued to change between the two post-infection time points. Although the PCA and sample-distance heatmap showed some variability among biological replicates, the Flu8 samples generally had the most distinct expression profiles, which is consistent with a stronger later response.

The enrichment results provided further insight into the biological processes underlying these changes. The dominant GO terms were related to interferon signaling, a major component of antiviral immunity. Enrichment of interferon-beta responses reflected type I interferon activity, while enrichment of type II interferon-related pathways suggested the involvement of additional immune-regulatory responses. Together, these findings indicate that antiviral defense pathways became a major part of the cerebellar response as the infection progressed.

KEGG analysis also identified enrichment of ether lipid, alpha-linolenic acid, and linoleic acid metabolism. These pathways are relevant because host lipids are involved in membrane organization, inflammatory signaling, viral-envelope formation, and influenza virus replication. The results therefore suggest that the response in cerebellar tissue was not limited to immune signaling but also involved changes in lipid-related transcriptional processes. Overall, the findings show that the effect of influenza A infection on cerebellar gene expression increased with time and was characterized by both antiviral interferon responses and changes in lipid-associated pathways.
